questions.prompt: How does a pytest test get access to a fixture?

options.text: By importing it at the top of the file
By listing the fixture's name as a parameter of the test function
By calling the fixture directly inside the test
By decorating the test with the fixture

questions.explanation: pytest injects a fixture when the test declares its name as a parameter; you don't call or import it.

questions.prompt: In a fixture that uses `yield`, where does teardown code go?

options.text: After the yield — and it runs even if the test fails
Teardown isn't possible with yield fixtures

questions.explanation: Setup runs before yield, teardown after; pytest guarantees the teardown runs after the test regardless of pass/fail.

questions.prompt: Order pytest fixture scopes from narrowest (most isolated) to widest (most shared).
questions.explanation: function (per test) is narrowest; module (per file) is wider; session (per run) is widest and most shared.

questions.prompt: Fixtures placed in a file named ____ are shared automatically across a directory tree without importing.
questions.explanation: conftest.py holds fixtures/hooks that pytest makes available to all tests in that directory and below.

questions.prompt: Which choices help prevent state leaking between tests? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep mutable fixtures at function scope
Use a session-scoped mutable list shared by all tests
Do teardown after yield so cleanup always runs

questions.explanation: Function scope, unique temp dirs, and guaranteed teardown all isolate tests; a wide-scope mutable object is exactly what causes leakage.

questions.prompt: Match each built-in fixture to what it provides.

pairs.right: A unique temporary directory per test
Safely set/replace attributes and env vars, auto-undone
Split a fixture into setup and teardown

questions.explanation: These built-ins cover temp files, patching, output capture, and the setup/teardown split.
